accuracy.evidence: The -s/-es rule matches the England Year 1 spelling appendix wording (ending heard as /s/ or /z/ is spelt -s; ending heard as /ɪz/ with an extra syllable is spelt -es) and CCSS L.K.1c (form regular plurals orally by adding /s/ or /es/). Every lab word was checked: fox, dish, bus, watch, box, wish, brush take -es; cup, hat, cat, pen, frog, bell, apple, hen take -s. Irregular plurals and y to ies are kept out on purpose and flagged as later learning in the adult text.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented Year 1 errors: over-applying -s to sibilant endings (foxs, wishs, boxs, buss), adding -es where no extra beat is heard (penes), adding an ending to one thing (1 apples, bananas), and treating any word ending in s as plural (bus, glass, grass) or a verb with s (takes) as a plural noun. The bus prediction and the find-the-plurals step attack the last one directly.

lab_distinct.evidence: Every step is about plural morphology itself: pens whose label gains a green s as the count passes one and loses it when it cycles back to 1, an -s/-es suffix tile dragged onto a stem, a syllable sort into one-clap and two-clap baskets, a sentence where only plural nouns light up, and a shop list with a no-ending option. Passed the 30% shingle gate against all other flagship labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees singular versus plural first (count 1 has no s), then meets the -es rule by its ending sounds, then discovers why the spelling differs by clapping the extra beat, then separates real plurals from look-alikes, and finally applies the full decision (none, -s or -es) to a counted list, the CCSS and NC evidence of choosing -s or -es by sound.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'two cat' versus 'two cats', 'foxs' versus 'foxes' (the over-generalised -s), and 'Is bus a plural? Yes, it ends in s' versus 'No, it is one bus'. The pens, the -es tiles and the bus tile then show the answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with ten distinct m= messages that name the slip: sh, x and s endings needing -es, no ending when there is more than one, frog singular versus plural, bus as one thing, -es wrongly added to pen, and an ending added when there is only 1 banana.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short read-aloud sentences with concrete nouns (cat, box, fox, bus, apple) and passes the family kid limit; adult text names Year 1, CCSS L.K.1c, sibilant endings and /ɪz/ within the adult limit. Canvas instructions are one short line; buttons are one emoji or one ending.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate. Kid paragraphs cover noun, plural with s, -es with the clap check, and one thing with no ending; adult paragraphs cover the standards, which endings take -es, named mistakes, and what the lab does; the family tip is one 'one, two' game.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots of every step at start and after Show me: three pens fit side by side with labels below, the -s and -es tiles fill the bottom row, the six word cards and two clap baskets fit without overlap, sentence tiles wrap to two lines, and the six shop rows sit above the three ending tiles; nothing clipped (phone_sweep found 0 findings).

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, every task completed with Show me, no console errors. Every drag or tap on the canvas has a button route (+1 per pen, -s/-es, clap buttons, word buttons, none/-s/-es), buttons carry aria-labels such as 'Add es to fox', and the canvas aria-label states the instruction and the result of each move.
